questions.question: How do you efficiently batch insert/update with JPA/Hibernate, and when should you drop to raw JDBC?
questions.title: JPA Batch Processing — Inserts, Updates, StatelessSession, COPY
questions.direct_answer: Default Hibernate sends **one SQL per `persist`/`merge`** — catastrophic for large batches. Enable batching with **`hibernate.jdbc.batch_size=50`** plus **`order_inserts`** and **`order_updates=true`**, switch generated IDs to **SEQUENCE** (IDENTITY blocks batching), and call **`em.flush(); em.clear()`** every N records to prevent first-level cache OOM. For very large loads, drop to **`StatelessSession`** (no persistence context), **`JdbcClient.batchUpdate`** (5–10× faster than JPA batch), or **Postgres `COPY`** (10M+ rows/minute). Wrap in a single transaction with chunked commits, disable second-level cache during imports, and consider dropping non-essential indexes for one-off migrations.

sections.title: Naive `save()` in a Loop Is the Single Worst Pattern in JPA
sections.content:
The textbook beginner code — `for (var dto : million) repo.save(toEntity(dto));` — looks innocent and is **catastrophically slow** in production.
- Every `save` triggers a round-trip: 1 million rows means 1 million SQL statements and 1 million network hops.
- Even on localhost the loop takes 10–30 minutes; over a managed cloud database it can run for hours.

The failure mode compounds.
- Hibernate's **first-level cache** retains every persisted entity in the persistence context, so memory grows linearly with the batch.
- **Dirty checking** at each flush iterates the entire managed set, turning a single large transaction into O(N²) CPU.
- And `@GeneratedValue(strategy = IDENTITY)` **silently disables JDBC batching** because Hibernate must read each generated key before issuing the next INSERT.

The fix is two-tiered: tune JPA batch settings for moderate volumes, and **drop down to `StatelessSession`, `JdbcClient.batchUpdate`, or Postgres `COPY`** when row counts cross hundreds of thousands. Knowing where each tool sits on the throughput curve is the difference between a 30-minute job and a 30-second one.

sections.content:


sections.title: Tuning JPA Batch — Configuration, Entity Mapping, and Loop Pattern
When to Drop to StatelessSession, JdbcClient, or Postgres COPY
Batch Strategies Side-by-Side
sections.content:
Pick the strategy that matches the row count, the need for domain logic, and the audit/cache requirements.

| Strategy | Throughput | Persistence context | Lifecycle callbacks | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Naive `repository.save()` loop | 10K–50K/min | Grows unboundedly | Fire | Demo code only |
| Tuned JPA batch (`batch_size=50` + flush/clear) | 100K–500K/min | Cleared per chunk | Fire | Domain entities, moderate volume |
| `StatelessSession` | 500K–800K/min | None | Skip | High-throughput inserts without callbacks |
| `JdbcClient.batchUpdate` | 1M–2M/min | None | Skip | Pure data ingest, no ORM needed |
| Postgres `COPY` | 10M+/min | None | Skip | Migrations, ETL, seed loads |

sections.title: The Pitfalls That Quietly Kill Batch Performance
sections.content:
**When tuning helps:**
- **Throughput jumps 10–50×** as soon as `batch_size`, `order_inserts`, and SEQUENCE IDs are aligned.
- **Heap stays flat** because `flush + clear` evicts entities each chunk.
- **Connection usage stays predictable** — one transaction, one connection, batched round-trips.

**When tuning hurts:**
- **`@DynamicUpdate` on hot entities** bypasses the prepared-statement cache and slows down high-frequency UPDATEs.
- **Oversized `batch_size`** (e.g., 10000) saturates the network buffer without improving throughput; sweet spot is 20–100.
- **Aggressive parallel workers** can deadlock on the same hot rows; serialize or partition by key.

**Pitfalls to watch for:**
- **`@GeneratedValue(IDENTITY)`** silently disables batching — switch to SEQUENCE.
- **Bidirectional `@OneToMany` with cascade** fires extra SQL per child; persist children explicitly or denormalize.
- **Second-level cache during import** — disable via `em.setProperty(QueryHints.HINT_CACHE_STOREMODE, CacheStoreMode.BYPASS)`.
- **Indexes on huge initial loads** — drop non-essential indexes, load, recreate; bulk index build is far faster.
- **Transaction sizing** — per-row commit is wasted overhead; one transaction per million rows produces WAL pressure and rollback risk; sweet spot is **10K–50K rows per commit**.
- **`@Version` columns** force `WHERE version = ?` on every UPDATE; keep `batch_versioned_data: true` enabled.
- **Lazy relationships triggered mid-batch** fire ad-hoc queries; use `StatelessSession` or fetch only the columns needed.
- **Auto-flush at query time** can drain the action queue prematurely — set `FlushModeType.COMMIT` in batch loops.
- **Memory pressure** — stream the source instead of holding all DTOs in memory; smaller batches (10–20) help on tight heaps.
- **No observability** — emit a `rows.imported` counter and log progress every chunk; alert when throughput drops.

sections.title: Production Bulk-Import Template with Per-Row Error Handling
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Naive save-in-a-loop** sends one SQL per row — switch to batch config plus flush/clear.
- **`hibernate.jdbc.batch_size=50` + `order_inserts` + `order_updates`** is the minimum viable tuning.
- **`@GeneratedValue(SEQUENCE)`** with `allocationSize` matching batch size; IDENTITY blocks batching entirely.
- **`em.flush(); em.clear()`** every batch prevents first-level cache OOM and O(N²) dirty checks.
- **Bulk JPQL `@Modifying`** issues one SQL but skips cascades, callbacks, and versioning.
- **`StatelessSession`** bypasses the persistence context — roughly 2× faster than tuned JPA batch.
- **`JdbcClient.batchUpdate`** is 5–10× faster than JPA batch for pure data ingest.
- **Postgres `COPY`** can load 10M+ rows/minute when domain logic is not required.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Default Hibernate sends one SQL per `persist` or `merge`, which is catastrophic for large batches. The fix is to tune the JDBC batch settings, change the ID generator, and clear the persistence context periodically.

**Why naive save-in-a-loop fails:**
- One round-trip per save — 1M rows is 1M SQL statements over the wire
- First-level cache grows unboundedly — multi-GB heap, then OOM
- Dirty checking at flush time is O(N²) over the managed set
- `@GeneratedValue(IDENTITY)` disables JDBC batching because Hibernate must read each ID first

**Tuning JPA batch:**
- `hibernate.jdbc.batch_size: 50` plus `order_inserts: true` and `order_updates: true`
- Switch to `@GeneratedValue(SEQUENCE)` with `allocationSize` matching batch size
- Loop with `em.persist(...)`, then `em.flush(); em.clear()` every 50 rows
- For UPDATE/DELETE on millions of rows, use `@Modifying @Query` for one-SQL bulk DML

**When to bypass JPA:**
- `StatelessSession` — no persistence context, no dirty checking; roughly 2× faster
- `JdbcClient.batchUpdate` (Spring 6.1+) — 5–10× faster, fluent API, no ORM overhead
- Postgres `COPY` via `CopyManager` — 10M+ rows per minute for migrations and ETL

**Production guard rails:**
- Commit every 10K–50K rows — balance atomicity against WAL pressure
- Disable second-level cache during imports (`CacheStoreMode.BYPASS`)
- Drop non-essential indexes for one-off migrations and recreate after
- Make the job idempotent with unique constraints or `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`
- Emit `rows.imported` and `rows.failed` metrics; alert when throughput drops

steps: Required application.yml: ``yaml spring: jpa: properties: hibernate: jdbc.batch_size: 50 order_inserts: true order_updates: true batch_versioned_data: true ` Why each flag matters: batch_size: 50 — instructs the JDBC driver to group statements into batched round-trips.
order_inserts: true — reorders pending INSERTs so same-table rows are contiguous; cross-table interleaving breaks batches.
batch_versioned_data: true — required for batching when entities use @Version (optimistic locking).

Entity mapping must use SEQUENCE, not IDENTITY: `java @Entity @Table(name = "orders") public class Order { @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = SEQUENCE, generator = "order_seq") @SequenceGenerator(name = "order_seq", sequenceName = "order_seq", allocationSize = 50) private Long id; } ` Why SEQUENCE wins: allocationSize = 50 matches batch_size, so Hibernate pre-allocates a block of IDs in one round-trip.
IDENTITY forces Hibernate to read each generated key after every INSERT — batching is impossible.
